course.title: React Native with Expo: 10 Real Projects
course.summary: Learn React Native from zero with Expo and TypeScript: ten complete apps with navigation, storage, SQLite, APIs, camera, notifications and state, plus testing and a store release guide.
course.description: Learn React Native with Expo and TypeScript by building 10 real apps with full source code, expected output, tests and an EAS publishing guide.

lessons.title: React Native with Expo: Setup and Your First App
lessons.metaTitle: React Native and Expo: Setup, First App
lessons.description: Learn what React Native and Expo are, install the tools, create a TypeScript project, run it on your phone with Expo Go, and understand the files Expo creates.

content.text: React Native lets you build real mobile apps for iPhone and Android with JavaScript or TypeScript and React. You write one codebase. The framework shows real native buttons, text boxes and lists on each phone, not a web page in disguise. That is why many companies use it: one team can ship to both stores, and web developers who already know React can move into mobile work quickly.

**Expo** is a set of tools on top of React Native. It gives you a ready project, a development server, ready-made libraries for the camera, files, notifications and more, and a build service. Today the React Native team itself recommends starting with Expo, so that is what this course uses. You do not need a Mac, and you do not need Xcode or Android Studio to start. You can test on your own phone with an app called Expo Go.
What you will build
After two lessons on the language and the core ideas, you build ten complete apps. Each uses a new group of skills that real teams use.

items: **Tip calculator**: components, state and styling.
**To-do list**: lists and saved data with AsyncStorage.
**Quiz**: several screens with Expo Router.
**Weather**: loading data from an API with loading and error states.
**Expense tracker**: useReducer, Context and money stored as cents.
**Notes**: a real SQLite database with search.
**Recipe browser**: TanStack Query for server data, caching and refresh.
**Photo journal**: camera, photo library, permissions and the file system.
**Habit tracker**: streaks and daily local notifications.
**Shop app**: Zustand for the cart and tab navigation.

content.text: The last lessons cover forms and security, testing and speed, and how to build and publish with EAS.

The code in this course was syntax-checked with a TypeScript parser. It was not run on a phone or emulator while the course was written, so type it in, run it with Expo and fix any small differences your versions show. React Native and Expo release often: when `npx expo install` picks newer library versions for you, accept them and read the release notes if something changes.
Install the tools

items: Install **Node.js** (the current LTS version) from the official Node website. It includes `npm`.
Install a code editor. **Visual Studio Code** is free and works well with TypeScript.
Install **Expo Go** on your phone from the App Store or Google Play.
Make sure your phone and your computer are on the same Wi-Fi network.

content.text: Create the project
**Terminal commands**

# Create the project (Node.js LTS must be installed)
npx create-expo-app@latest my-app --template blank-typescript
cd my-app
npx expo start
# press a for Android emulator, i for iOS simulator (macOS), or scan the QR code with the Expo Go app

The first command creates a folder with a blank TypeScript app. The second starts the development server and prints a QR code. On Android open Expo Go and scan it. On iPhone scan it with the Camera app. The app loads on your phone in a few seconds. Edit a file and save, and the phone updates by itself. This is called **Fast Refresh**, and it makes learning quick.
What Expo created

my-app/
  App.tsx          the first screen (older template; newer ones use app/)
  app.json         app name, icon, version, permissions and plugins
  package.json     libraries (dependencies) and scripts
  tsconfig.json    TypeScript settings
  assets/          icons and images
  node_modules/    installed libraries (never edit)
Open `App.tsx`. You will see something like this.

`App` is a **component**: a function that returns what should appear on screen. `View` is a box, like a `div`. `Text` shows text, and all text in React Native must be inside `Text`. `StyleSheet.create` holds the styles as plain objects. The syntax that looks like HTML inside the function is **JSX**, which React turns into native elements.

If your phone cannot connect, press `s` in the terminal to switch connection mode, or start with `npx expo start --tunnel`. You can also press `a` to open an Android emulator or `i` for the iOS simulator on a Mac.
Your task

items: Install Node.js and Expo Go, then create the project and scan the QR code.
Change the text to your name and save. Watch the phone update.
Add a second `Text` line and give the first one a bigger `fontSize` in the styles.
Open `app.json` and find the app name.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The app shows on your phone and updates when you save.
You can say what a component, JSX and Expo each are.

steps.say: You write TypeScript and React components.
The dev server bundles your code and sends it to the phone over Wi-Fi.
Expo Go on the phone runs the JavaScript.
React Native draws real native views. Save a file and the screen refreshes.

faqs.q: Do I need a Mac to build iPhone apps?
faqs.a: You can develop and test on iPhone with Expo Go from Windows or Linux. A Mac is not needed for builds either, because EAS Build compiles iOS apps in the cloud, though you need an Apple Developer account to publish.

faqs.q: Is React Native the same as React?
faqs.a: They share the same ideas: components, props, state and hooks. React draws web pages, while React Native draws native mobile views using components like View and Text.

faqs.q: Expo or bare React Native?
faqs.a: Start with Expo. It covers most apps and you can add custom native code later with development builds when a library requires it.

quiz.q: What does React Native draw on the phone?
options: A web page in a hidden browser

quiz.q: What is Expo Go?
options: An app that runs your project on your phone during development

quiz.q: What is Fast Refresh?
options: The app updates on the phone when you save a file

lessons.title: JavaScript and TypeScript Essentials for React Native
lessons.metaTitle: JavaScript and TypeScript for React Native
lessons.description: Learn the JavaScript and TypeScript React Native needs: const and let, arrow functions, array methods, destructuring, spread, types and async await.

content.text: React Native is written in JavaScript, and in this course in TypeScript, which is JavaScript with types. You do not need to master the language first. You need a working set of ideas that appear in every app. This lesson teaches them with small programs. To run them, create a file such as `demo.ts` in any folder and run `npx tsx demo.ts`, or paste the code into the online TypeScript Playground.
Variables and types

Use `const` for values that are never reassigned and `let` for values that change. Avoid the old `var`. TypeScript infers most types from the value, and you add a type where it is not obvious, mainly on function parameters and on objects that other code uses. Backticks make template strings, where `${...}` inserts a value.

Asha walked 6500 steps
That is 65% of the goal
Functions, arrays and types

Arrow functions are short functions. Array methods are the main tool for working with lists: `filter` keeps items, `map` changes every item, `reduce` folds them into one value. They return new arrays and do not change the old one. In React you always create new arrays and objects instead of changing existing ones, because React compares them to decide what to redraw. A `type` describes the shape of an object, and `?` marks an optional field.

Hello, Ravi!
Welcome, Ravi!
[ 75, 90, 55 ]
[ 150, 180, 110 ]
260
Destructuring and spread

Destructuring pulls values out of objects and arrays into variables. The spread operator `...` copies an object or array and lets you change part of it. You will use `{ ...item, done: true }` constantly to update state.

Meera Pune
React [ 'TypeScript' ]
Delhi Pune
Async code

Network calls and storage take time, so they return a **Promise**: a value that arrives later. `async` functions use `await` to wait for a promise while the rest of the app keeps running. Put the awaited code in `try/catch` to handle errors.

User 7
Failed: Bad id
All the expected outputs here were worked out by hand from the code. Run each sample to confirm them.
Why this matters in React Native

items: State updates use spread and `map` to build new objects and lists.
Every API call, database call and permission request is async.
Types catch mistakes such as passing a number where text is expected, before you run the app.
Optional fields and `?.` stop crashes when data is missing.

content.text: Your task

items: Run all four samples and compare the output.
Write a type `Product` with name and price, a list of three products and print the names of those above 100.
Write an async function that waits 200 ms and returns a number, call it and print the result.
Use destructuring to read `city` from an object that may not have it, with a default value.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Your outputs match the lesson.
You can explain why React code copies arrays instead of changing them.
You know what `await` does and where to put `try/catch`.

steps.say: You have an array of scores.
filter returns a new array with only the scores of 50 or more.
map returns another new array with each value doubled.
The original array is untouched. React relies on this habit.

faqs.q: Do I have to use TypeScript?
faqs.a: No, React Native works with plain JavaScript. TypeScript is worth it because it finds many mistakes before you run the app, and most teams use it.

faqs.q: const or let?
faqs.a: Use const by default. Use let only when the variable must be reassigned. Objects and arrays declared with const can still have their contents changed, but in React you avoid doing that.

faqs.q: What is a Promise?
faqs.a: A Promise is a value that will be available later, such as the result of a network request. await pauses an async function until it is ready.

quiz.q: Which keyword should you use by default for a value that is never reassigned?
What does map return?
What does await do?
options: Pauses an async function until a promise is ready

lessons.title: Core Components, State and Project 1: Tip Calculator
lessons.description: Learn View, Text, TextInput, Pressable, FlatList, StyleSheet and Flexbox, then useState, and build a complete tip calculator in React Native with a test.

content.text: A React Native screen is built from components. A few built-in ones cover most needs, and you combine them. This lesson teaches them and the idea of state, then builds your first complete app.
The core components

items: **View**: a box that groups and positions other things.
**Text**: all visible text. Text cannot sit directly inside a View.
**TextInput**: a box to type in. Use `value` and `onChangeText`. `keyboardType` picks the keyboard.
**Pressable**: anything that can be tapped. It replaces the old TouchableOpacity for most uses.
**Image**: shows a picture from a file or a web address. Remote images need a width and a height.
**ScrollView and FlatList**: ScrollView shows everything at once. FlatList draws only the rows on screen, so use it for long lists.
**Switch, ActivityIndicator, Modal**: a toggle, a spinner and a pop-up panel.
**SafeAreaView**: keeps content away from notches and system bars.

content.text: Styling and Flexbox

Styles are JavaScript objects, written with `StyleSheet.create`. Layout uses **Flexbox**, with two differences from the web: the default direction is vertical (`column`), and sizes are numbers without units. `flexDirection: "row"` puts children side by side. `justifyContent` places them along the main direction, `alignItems` across it, `flex: 1` makes an item take the available space, and `gap` adds space between children.
State: data that changes the screen
`useState` gives a component a value that can change. When you call the setter, React runs the component again with the new value and updates only what changed.

const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
<Pressable onPress={() => setCount(count + 1)}>
  <Text>Clicked {count} times</Text>
</Pressable>
Never change state directly (`count++`). Always call the setter with a new value. When the new value depends on the old one, use the function form `setCount((c) => c + 1)`.
Project 1: Tip Calculator
The user types a bill, chooses a tip, sets how many people share and sees the totals. All the maths lives in a plain function in its own file, so you can test it without a phone.
No extra libraries are needed for this project.

my-app/
  App.tsx        the screen
  tip.ts         the calculation, with no React in it
  __tests__/
    tip.test.ts
    TipScreen.test.tsx
**`tip.ts`**
**`App.tsx`**
How it works

items: Four values are in state: the bill text, tip percent, number of people and the round-up switch.
The bill stays as text because the user types it. `parseFloat(billText) || 0` turns empty or invalid text into 0.
The result is calculated on every render, so it can never be out of date.
The array `[10, 15, 20, 25].map(...)` creates one button for each tip choice. Each needs a unique `key`.

content.text: Expected output

The screen shows the title, a bill box, four tip buttons with 15% highlighted, a people row showing 1, a round-up switch and a card. Type 100: the card shows Tip 15.00, Total 115.00 and Each person pays 115.00. Press + twice: each person pays 38.33. With a bill of 33 and 15%, the tip is 4.95, and 5.00 when round up is on.

The code in this course was syntax-checked with a TypeScript parser. It was not run on a phone or emulator while the course was written, so type it in, run it with Expo and fix any small differences your versions show. React Native and Expo release often: when `npx expo install` picks newer library versions for you, accept them and read the release notes if something changes.
Your task

items: Create the project, add the two files and run the app.
Check the three examples.
Add a custom tip box where the user types their own percent.
Run the tests in the testing lesson later and add one for your custom tip.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: 100 at 15% gives a total of 115.00.
The numbers change as you tap, with no calculate button.
You can explain what useState does and why we never change state directly.

steps.say: The user types a bill or taps a tip button.
The handler calls a state setter with the new value.
React runs the component function again with the new state.
The new JSX is compared with the old one, and only the changes are applied to the screen.

faqs.q: Why do list items need a key?
faqs.a: The key tells React which item is which when the list changes, so it can update the right rows and keep their state. Use a stable ID, not the array index, when items can move.

faqs.q: Why can't I put text directly inside a View?
faqs.a: On phones, text is drawn by a special native component. React Native requires all text to be inside Text.

faqs.q: View or Pressable?
faqs.a: Use View to lay things out and Pressable when the user must tap it. Pressable adds press events and pressed-state styling.

quiz.q: Where must all visible text be placed?
What is the default flex direction in React Native?
How should you update state?
options: Call the setter with a new value

lessons.title: Project 2: To-Do List with FlatList and AsyncStorage
lessons.description: Build a to-do app in React Native with FlatList, useEffect and AsyncStorage so tasks stay saved after the app closes, with full code.

content.text: The tip calculator forgot everything when you closed it. A to-do app must remember. This project adds three ideas: showing a list with **FlatList**, running code at the right moment with **useEffect**, and saving small data on the phone with **AsyncStorage**.
Concepts in this project

items: **FlatList**: draws only visible rows. You pass `data`, a `keyExtractor` that returns a unique string, and `renderItem`. `ListEmptyComponent` shows a message when the list is empty.
**useEffect**: runs code after the screen draws. With `[]` it runs once at start (load saved tasks). With `[todos]` it runs whenever tasks change (save them).
**AsyncStorage**: a simple key-value store that keeps text on the phone. Store objects with `JSON.stringify` and read them with `JSON.parse`.
**Immutable updates**: `map` to change one item, `filter` to remove, spread to add. Never push into the existing array.

content.text: Create the project

items: Create a new Expo project, or reuse your first one.
Install the storage library with `npx expo install @react-native-async-storage/async-storage`.
Add `storage.ts` and replace `App.tsx`.

content.text:
my-app/
  App.tsx       list, input, buttons
  storage.ts    load and save functions
The code
**`storage.ts`**
`loadTodos` returns an empty list if nothing was saved or if reading fails, so the app never crashes on a damaged value.
**`App.tsx`**
How it works

items: The first `useEffect` loads saved tasks once and then sets `ready`.
The second saves tasks every time they change, but only after `ready`, so the empty starting list does not overwrite saved data.
`add`, `toggle`, `remove` and `clearDone` each build a new list.
`left` is calculated while rendering from `todos`. It is not stored separately, so it cannot be wrong.

content.text: Expected output

You see the title, a text box with an Add button, the line "0 left, 0 done" and the message "Nothing to do. Add your first task above." Add Buy milk and Call Dad: both appear, and the line reads "2 left, 0 done". Tap Buy milk: it gets a line through it and the line reads "1 left, 1 done". A Clear finished tasks link appears. Close the app fully and open it again: the tasks are still there.
AsyncStorage is for small data. For thousands of rows or for searching, use SQLite (project 6). Do not store passwords or tokens in it. Use secure storage (lesson 13).

The code in this course was syntax-checked with a TypeScript parser. It was not run on a phone or emulator while the course was written, so type it in, run it with Expo and fix any small differences your versions show. Always install Expo libraries with `npx expo install` so the versions match your Expo SDK.
Your task

items: Build the app and check the example. Then force-close the app and reopen it.
Add an edit feature: tapping the task title opens it in the text box.
Show "All done, well done!" when every task is ticked.
Sort tasks so unfinished ones come first.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Tasks survive closing the app.
Ticking, deleting and clearing all work and the counter updates.
You can explain why the save effect waits for ready.

steps.say: The user adds or ticks a task. The handler creates a new array.
The state changed, so the save effect runs.
The effect writes the list as JSON text.
Next time the app opens, the load effect reads it back into state.

faqs.q: What does the empty array in useEffect mean?
faqs.a: It means the effect has no dependencies, so it runs once after the first render. It is the usual place to load saved data.

faqs.q: Why not push into the array?
faqs.a: React decides to redraw by comparing old and new values. If you change the same array, the reference is unchanged and React may not notice. A new array always triggers an update.

faqs.q: Can AsyncStorage lose data?
faqs.a: It can if the user clears app data or the phone is reset. Treat it as a local cache and use a server or backup for data that must never be lost.

quiz.q: When does useEffect with an empty array run?
Why not push into the existing state array?
options: React may not notice the change; a new array triggers a redraw

quiz.q: What is AsyncStorage best for?
options: Small data kept on the phone

lessons.title: Project 3: Quiz App with Expo Router
lessons.metaTitle: Project 3: Quiz App with Expo Router
lessons.description: Build a multi-screen quiz app with Expo Router: file based routes, Stack navigation, route params, router.push and replace, with complete TypeScript code.

content.text: Real apps have many screens. In Expo, the standard way to move between them is **Expo Router**. It uses file-based routing, like Next.js on the web: each file in the `app` folder becomes a screen, and its name becomes the route. It is built on React Navigation, so you get native-feeling transitions and a back button for free.
Concepts in this project

items: **File-based routes**: `app/index.tsx` is `/`, `app/quiz.tsx` is `/quiz`, `app/[id].tsx` is `/123`.
**_layout.tsx**: wraps the screens in a navigator. `Stack` pushes screens on top of each other.
**useRouter**: `router.push` goes forward, `router.replace` swaps the current screen, `router.back` goes back.
**Params**: send values with `{ pathname, params }` and read them with `useLocalSearchParams`. Params are always strings.
**Keep data out of `app/`**: every file there is treated as a route, so put helpers in a `src` folder.

content.text: Set up Expo Router
A new project made with the default Expo template already uses Expo Router. If you started from the blank template, follow these steps.
**package.json, app.json and folder layout**
Install the supporting libraries with the commands below (use only the lines you need now), and delete the old `App.tsx` so it does not conflict.
**Install commands for all ten projects**

# Install libraries with expo install so versions match your Expo SDK
npx expo install @react-native-async-storage/async-storage   # projects 2, 5, 8, 9
npx expo install expo-router react-native-safe-area-context react-native-screens expo-linking expo-constants expo-status-bar   # projects 3, 7, 10
npx expo install expo-sqlite                                  # project 6
npx expo install expo-image-picker expo-file-system           # project 8
npx expo install expo-notifications                           # project 9
npm install @tanstack/react-query zustand                     # projects 7, 10
Each project tells you which line to run.

my-app/
  app/
    _layout.tsx    Stack navigator
    index.tsx      home: Start button
    quiz.tsx       questions
    result.tsx     final score
  src/
    questions.ts   the quiz data
The code
**`src/questions.ts`**
**`app/_layout.tsx`**
**`app/index.tsx`**
**`app/quiz.tsx`**
**`app/result.tsx`**
How it works

items: Start calls `router.push("/quiz")`. The stack now holds home and quiz.

The quiz keeps `index`, `score` and the chosen answer in state. After the last question it calls `router.replace` to `/result` with the score as params. `replace` swaps the quiz out so Back does not return to it.
The result screen reads `score` and `total` with `useLocalSearchParams` and offers Play again with `router.replace("/")`.

content.text: Expected output

The home screen shows React Native Quiz, "4 questions" and a Start button. Each question shows Question 1 of 4, the text and four options. Tapping an option turns the right answer green and a wrong choice red, and a Next button appears. After the last question you see "You scored 3 out of 4" (your number depends on your answers) and a Play again button. The back arrow is hidden on the quiz and result screens by design.

The code in this course was syntax-checked with a TypeScript parser. It was not run on a phone or emulator while the course was written, so type it in, run it with Expo and fix any small differences your versions show. Always install Expo libraries with `npx expo install` so the versions match your Expo SDK.
Your task

items: Set up the router, add the files and play the quiz.
Add four more questions to `src/questions.ts`.
Show a different message for a perfect score on the result screen.
Add a Settings screen reachable from home and check that the back button returns to home.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The quiz runs from start to result.
Back does not return into a finished quiz.
You can explain push versus replace.

steps.say: Every file in app/ becomes a route automatically.
The layout wraps them in a Stack navigator.
router.push opens the quiz screen on top of home.
At the end router.replace opens the result with the score as params.

faqs.q: Why use Expo Router instead of React Navigation directly?
faqs.a: Expo Router builds on React Navigation and adds file-based routes and deep links. It means less setup and URLs for every screen, which helps with links and the web.

faqs.q: Why are route params strings?
faqs.a: Params travel in the URL, so they are text. Convert them with Number() or JSON when you need another type, and pass an ID instead of a whole object.

faqs.q: Where do non-screen files go?
faqs.a: Outside the app folder, for example in src, because every file in app is treated as a screen.

quiz.q: In Expo Router, what makes a route?
options: A file inside the app folder

quiz.q: What does router.replace do compared with push?
options: Swaps the current screen instead of stacking a new one

quiz.q: What type are route params?

lessons.title: Project 4: Weather App with fetch and Error States
lessons.description: Build a weather app that loads live data from a free API with fetch and async await, using a TypeScript union type for idle, loading, error and success states.

content.text: Most apps talk to servers. This project loads live weather and teaches the pattern that every data screen needs: show a spinner while waiting, show data on success and show a clear message on failure. You use the built-in `fetch` function, with no extra library.
Concepts in this project

items: **REST API and JSON**: you request a URL and get text in JSON form, which `res.json()` turns into an object.
**fetch and async/await**: `await fetch(url)` waits without freezing the screen. Check `res.ok`, because fetch does not throw on HTTP errors like 404.
**Union types for state**: `idle | loading | error | ok`. Each case carries only the data that makes sense. TypeScript makes sure you handle each one.

**Two requests**: first look up the city's coordinates with the free Open-Meteo geocoding endpoint, then ask for the weather at those coordinates. No API key is needed. Check the service's current terms and URLs before you build.
**Separation**: the network code is in its own file. The screen only shows state.

content.text: Create the project

items: Use a blank Expo TypeScript project. No extra library is needed.
Add `weather.ts` and replace `App.tsx`.

content.text: **`weather.ts`**
**`App.tsx`**
How it works

items: `fetchWeather` throws an `Error` with a friendly message at each failure point. The screen only has to catch it.
`search` sets `loading`, awaits the data, then sets `ok` or `error`.
The screen renders one block for each kind of state with simple `&&` checks.
`encodeURIComponent` makes the city name safe to put in a URL (for example, for names with spaces).

content.text: Expected output

You see a search box and a Search button. Type London and press Search. A spinner shows briefly, then a card with London, GB, a large temperature such as 11°C, a description such as Partly cloudy and the wind speed. The numbers are live and will differ from this example. Type a nonsense word and the app shows "City not found". Turn on airplane mode and search again: a short error message appears and the app keeps running.
Never put a secret API key in a mobile app. Anything inside the app can be extracted. This project uses a keyless API. For a service that needs a key, call it from your own server.

The code in this course was syntax-checked with a TypeScript parser. It was not run on a phone or emulator while the course was written, so type it in, run it with Expo and fix any small differences your versions show. Always install Expo libraries with `npx expo install` so the versions match your Expo SDK.
Your task

items: Build the app and search three cities.
Test the error paths: a nonsense city and airplane mode.
Show an emoji next to the description using a lookup table keyed by weather code.
Remember the last city with AsyncStorage and search for it when the app opens.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: A real city shows live data.
Errors show a message, never a crash.
You can explain why `res.ok` must be checked.

steps.say: The user presses Search and the state becomes loading.
The async function calls fetch and waits.
The server answers with JSON, or the request fails.
The state becomes ok with data, or error with a message, and the screen shows it.

faqs.q: Why doesn't fetch throw on a 404?
faqs.a: fetch only rejects when the network request itself fails. A 404 or 500 is still a response, so you must check res.ok and throw your own error.

faqs.q: Why use a union type for state?
faqs.a: It makes impossible states impossible, such as loading and error at once. TypeScript also warns you if you forget to handle a case.

faqs.q: Axios or fetch?
faqs.a: fetch is built in and enough for most apps. Axios adds conveniences like interceptors. For caching and retries, use TanStack Query on top of either, as in project 7.

quiz.q: Why check res.ok after fetch?
options: fetch does not throw on HTTP errors like 404

quiz.q: What does a union type for state help with?
options: Making impossible states impossible and handling each case

quiz.q: Why should a secret API key stay out of the app?
options: Anything in the app can be extracted

lessons.title: Project 5: Expense Tracker with useReducer and Context
lessons.description: Build an expense tracker with useReducer, Context and AsyncStorage, store money as whole cents and group spending by category with useMemo.

content.text: This project grows the state of an app. A reducer puts all changes to the list in one place, and Context shares that state with any screen without passing props down by hand. It also introduces a rule every serious app follows: handle money as integers.
Concepts in this project

items: **useReducer**: you describe changes as actions, such as `add` and `remove`, and one `reducer` function returns the next state. It is easier to follow and test than many setters.
**Context**: `createContext` and a Provider make state available to the whole tree. A custom hook, `useExpenses`, hides the details and throws a clear error if used outside the provider.
**Money as cents**: floating point cannot store values like 0.1 exactly, so 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004. Store whole cents and format at the edge.
**useMemo**: caches a calculated value, like totals per category, until its inputs change.
**Validation**: `parseCents` returns `null` for bad input, which the form turns into a message.

content.text: Create the project

items: Use a blank Expo TypeScript project and install AsyncStorage with `npx expo install @react-native-async-storage/async-storage`.
Add three files.

content.text:
my-app/
  App.tsx
  ExpenseContext.tsx   reducer, provider, useExpenses hook
  money.ts             parseCents and asMoney
**`money.ts`**
**`ExpenseContext.tsx`**
**`App.tsx`**
How it works

items: The reducer handles three actions: `load`, `add`, `remove`. Each returns a new state object.
The provider loads from AsyncStorage once and saves every time the state changes after loading.
The screen reads the state with `useExpenses()` and sends actions with `dispatch`.
The form checks the amount with `parseCents`, so an empty box or text such as "abc" shows an error and never reaches the list.

content.text: Expected output

The top shows a big total, 0.00 at first. Add Lunch 12.50 in Food, Bus 3.20 in Travel and Coffee 4.00 in Food. The total reads 19.70 and the summary lines read Food: 16.50 and Travel: 3.20. The list shows three items, newest first. Remove Coffee and the total becomes 15.70. Close and reopen the app: the data remains. Entering abc shows "Enter a title and an amount such as 12.50".

The code in this course was syntax-checked with a TypeScript parser. It was not run on a phone or emulator while the course was written, so type it in, run it with Expo and fix any small differences your versions show. Always install Expo libraries with `npx expo install` so the versions match your Expo SDK.
Your task

items: Build the app and reproduce the numbers above.
Add a monthly budget input and colour the total red above it.
Add a `date` field to each expense and show this month's total.
Run the money tests from the testing lesson against `money.ts`.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Totals always equal the sum of the list.
Amounts never show floating-point noise.
You can explain what a reducer and an action are.

steps.say: The user adds an expense. The screen dispatches an action.
The reducer receives the old state and the action.
It returns a brand new state with the item added.
Every component that uses the context redraws with the new list and totals.

faqs.q: useReducer or useState?
faqs.a: Use useState for simple independent values. Use useReducer when several actions change the same data, because the rules then live in one tested function.

faqs.q: Is Context a replacement for a state library?
faqs.a: For modest apps, yes. Context re-renders every consumer when its value changes, so large or fast-changing state may need a store such as Zustand (project 10).

faqs.q: Why are cents safer than decimals?
faqs.a: Whole numbers are exact. Rounding only happens once, when you display the value.

quiz.q: What does a reducer return?
Why store money as cents?
What does useMemo do?
options: Caches a calculated value until its inputs change

lessons.title: Project 6: Notes App with expo-sqlite
lessons.description: Build a notes app with expo-sqlite: create a table, insert, update, delete and search with SQL, with a Modal editor and a floating button.

content.text: When your data has many rows, relationships or needs searching and sorting, a real database is the right tool. SQLite is a small database that lives in a file on the phone, and Expo provides it through **expo-sqlite**. You write SQL, and your data survives app restarts.
Concepts in this project

items: **SQL basics**: `CREATE TABLE` defines columns, `INSERT` adds a row, `UPDATE` changes one, `DELETE` removes one and `SELECT ... WHERE ... ORDER BY` reads.
**Parameters**: put `?` in the SQL and pass the values in an array. This avoids SQL injection and quoting problems. Never join user text into SQL yourself.
**Async API**: `openDatabaseAsync`, `execAsync`, `runAsync` and `getAllAsync` all return promises.
**A small data layer**: all SQL is in `db.ts`. The screen calls `listNotes`, `saveNote` and `deleteNote` and knows nothing about SQL.
**Modal**: a pop-up screen used here as the editor.

content.text: Create the project

items: Use a blank Expo TypeScript project and install the library: `npx expo install expo-sqlite`.
Add `db.ts` and replace `App.tsx`.

content.text: `getDb` opens the database once and creates the table if it is missing, then reuses the same connection. `listNotes` filters with `LIKE` and sorts the newest first.
**`App.tsx`**
How it works

items: `refresh` runs the query for the current search text. The effect calls it at the start and whenever the text changes, so results narrow as you type.
Tapping a note opens the editor with its values. The + button opens it empty.
`saveNote` updates when the note has an `id`, and inserts otherwise.
Long-pressing a note deletes it.

content.text: Expected output

The first screen shows Notes, a search box and the message "No notes yet. Tap + to add one." Tap +, enter a title and text and press Save: the note appears. Add two more. Type a word from one note in the search box and only the matching notes remain. Tap a note to edit it and save: it moves to the top because it has the newest update time. Long-press to delete. Close and reopen the app: the notes are still there.

If you change the table later (add a column), you need a migration, such as `ALTER TABLE notes ADD COLUMN pinned INTEGER DEFAULT 0`, run when the app starts. During development you can also uninstall the app to reset the database.

The code in this course was syntax-checked with a TypeScript parser. It was not run on a phone or emulator while the course was written, so type it in, run it with Expo and fix any small differences your versions show. Always install Expo libraries with `npx expo install` so the versions match your Expo SDK.
Your task

items: Build the app and add three notes, then search.
Add a `pinned` column and show pinned notes first.
Ask the user to confirm before a long-press delete using `Alert.alert`.
Show the update date on each card.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Notes persist after closing the app.
Search narrows the list as you type.
All SQL uses `?` parameters.

steps.say: The user saves a note. The screen calls saveNote.
The data layer runs an INSERT or UPDATE with ? parameters.
SQLite writes the row to the file.
The screen calls listNotes again and shows the fresh result.

faqs.q: AsyncStorage or SQLite?
faqs.a: Use AsyncStorage for small settings and simple lists. Use SQLite for many rows, searching, sorting and relationships.

faqs.q: Why use ? placeholders?
faqs.a: The library sends the values separately from the SQL, so user text can never change the meaning of the query. This blocks SQL injection.

faqs.q: How do I keep the screen updated automatically?
faqs.a: In this project you call refresh after each change. Larger apps wrap queries in TanStack Query or use a library that observes the database.

quiz.q: Why use ? placeholders in SQL?
options: Values are sent separately, which blocks SQL injection

quiz.q: When is SQLite a better choice than AsyncStorage?
What do you need if you add a column to a released app?

lessons.title: Project 7: Recipe Browser with Query
lessons.description: Build a recipe browser with TanStack Query: caching, loading and error states, pull to refresh and a dynamic Expo Router detail screen.

content.text: In project 4 you wrote loading and error state by hand. In a bigger app you do that on many screens, and you also want caching, retries and refresh. **TanStack Query** (formerly React Query) is the standard library for server data. You describe what to fetch, and it handles state, caching and updates. It is one of the most useful tools to learn for a React Native job.
Concepts in this project

items: **useQuery**: takes a `queryKey` (the identity of the data) and a `queryFn` (how to fetch it). It returns `data`, `isLoading`, `isError`, `error`, `refetch` and `isRefetching`.
**Caching**: the same key shows cached data instantly. `staleTime` says how long data counts as fresh.
**QueryClientProvider**: put it at the top of the app, here in the root layout.
**Dynamic routes**: `app/[id].tsx` matches any ID. Read it with `useLocalSearchParams`.
**Mapping messy data**: TheMealDB returns ingredients as `strIngredient1`, `strIngredient2` and so on. `getMeal` collects them into a clean list.
**Data source**: TheMealDB with its public test key. Check its current terms and that the test key still works before you build.

content.text: Create the project

items: Use an Expo Router project (see project 3).
Install the library: `npm install @tanstack/react-query`.
Add the files shown.

content.text:
my-app/
  app/
    _layout.tsx    QueryClientProvider + Stack
    index.tsx      search and list
    [id].tsx       recipe detail
  src/
    api.ts         searchMeals and getMeal
**`src/api.ts`**
**`app/_layout.tsx`**
**`app/index.tsx`**
**`app/[id].tsx`**
How it works

items: The search screen keeps the box text and the submitted `term` separately. Only when the user submits does `term` change, which changes the query key and triggers a new fetch.
Going back to a term you already searched shows cached results immediately.
Pulling the list down calls `refetch`. `isRefetching` drives the spinner.
The detail screen uses `enabled: !!id` so the query only runs when the ID exists.

content.text: Expected output

The app opens on a Recipes screen and searches "chicken" by itself. A list of recipes with pictures appears. Search for "pasta" and press the search key: a new list loads. Search for "chicken" again: the old list appears instantly from the cache. Tap a recipe to see a large picture, its category and area, the ingredients with measures and the instructions. Turn on airplane mode and search a new word: the app shows an error message and does not crash.

The code in this course was syntax-checked with a TypeScript parser. It was not run on a phone or emulator while the course was written, so type it in, run it with Expo and fix any small differences your versions show. Always install Expo libraries with `npx expo install` so the versions match your Expo SDK.
Your task

items: Build the app and search three words, then repeat the first one.
Add a Retry button to the error state.
Add a heart button that stores favourite IDs in AsyncStorage and a Favourites screen.
Turn on the React Native debugging tools and watch the query states while you search.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Repeated searches show cached data at once.
Pull to refresh reloads the list.
You can explain what a query key is.

steps.say: The screen asks for the data with a query key.
If the key is already cached and fresh, the cache answers instantly.
Otherwise the query function fetches and cleans the data.
The result is stored in the cache and the screen redraws with it.

faqs.q: Why use TanStack Query instead of useEffect and fetch?
faqs.a: It gives you loading and error state, caching, retries, refetching and deduplicated requests with very little code. You avoid many bugs that hand-written effects have.

faqs.q: What is a query key?
faqs.a: It is the identity of the data, usually an array such as ["meals", term]. When the key changes, the library fetches again, and when it repeats, it can reuse the cache.

faqs.q: What is staleTime?
faqs.a: It is how long fetched data counts as fresh. During that time the library will not refetch it automatically.

quiz.q: What is a query key?
options: The identity of the data, such as ["meals", term]

quiz.q: What happens when you repeat a search that is cached and fresh?
options: It always waits for the server

quiz.q: What does enabled: !!id do?
options: Runs the query only when the id exists

lessons.title: Project 8: Photo Journal with Camera and File System
lessons.description: Build a photo journal with expo-image-picker and expo-file-system: ask for camera and library permissions, copy photos into app storage and save captions.

content.text: Phones have a camera, a photo library and file storage, and apps use them constantly. This project teaches how to use device features safely. The most important lesson is permissions. The user must agree before your app uses the camera or photos, and your app must still work when they say no.
Concepts in this project

items: **expo-image-picker**: opens the photo library or the camera. It returns a temporary file address (`uri`).
**Permissions**: call `requestCameraPermissionsAsync` or `requestMediaLibraryPermissionsAsync` and check `granted`. Explain, with `Alert`, what to do when permission is denied.
**expo-file-system**: copy the picked photo into the app's own document folder so it stays after the temporary file is cleaned up.
**Metadata in AsyncStorage**: the caption, date and file address for each entry.
**Cleaning up**: delete the file when the entry is deleted, so storage does not fill with orphan photos.
**Permission texts**: iOS shows a message you write in `app.json`. Use clear, honest text.

content.text: Create the project

items: Use a blank Expo TypeScript project.
Install the libraries: `npx expo install expo-image-picker expo-file-system @react-native-async-storage/async-storage`.
Add the permission texts to `app.json` (below).
Add `journal.ts` and replace `App.tsx`.

content.text: **app.json permission texts**
**`journal.ts`**
**`App.tsx`**
How it works

items: `add` first asks for permission, then opens the picker or the camera. If the user cancels, nothing happens.
`addEntry` copies the temporary photo into the `photos/` folder with a new name and saves the entry list.
The list shows each photo with its caption and date. Delete removes the file and the entry.
The camera works on a real phone. Emulators may only have a simulated camera.

content.text: API names in Expo libraries change between SDK versions. For example, newer versions of file system have a newer object-based API alongside the classic functions used here. If an import is reported as deprecated, check that library's page in the Expo docs for the current names.
Expected output

The screen shows Photo Journal, a caption box and two buttons, Choose photo and Take photo. Tap Choose photo: the system asks permission the first time. Allow it, pick a photo and it appears as a card with your caption and today's date. Add another with the camera. Close and reopen the app: both entries are still there with their photos. Delete one and it disappears. If you deny permission, the app shows an alert and keeps working.

The code in this course was syntax-checked with a TypeScript parser. It was not run on a phone or emulator while the course was written, so type it in, run it with Expo and fix any small differences your versions show. Always install Expo libraries with `npx expo install` so the versions match your Expo SDK.
Your task

items: Build the app on a real phone and add one photo from the library and one from the camera.
Deny permission once and read the alert. Then allow it in the phone's Settings and try again.
Tap a photo to show it full screen in a Modal.
Add a search box that filters entries by caption.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Photos remain after the app restarts.
Denied permission produces a message, not a crash.
Deleting an entry also removes its file.

steps.say: The user taps Take photo.
The app asks for camera permission and stops with a message if it is denied.
If it is allowed, the picker opens the camera and returns a temporary file address.
The app copies the file into its own folder and saves the caption and date.

faqs.q: Why copy the photo?
faqs.a: The picker gives a temporary address that the system may clear. Copying it into the app's document folder keeps it as long as the app is installed.

faqs.q: What if the user denies permission forever?
faqs.a: On many systems the request cannot be shown again. Explain what the feature needs and offer a button that opens the app's settings using Linking.openSettings().

faqs.q: Does the camera work in Expo Go?
faqs.a: Yes on a real phone for the picker and camera used here. Some libraries need a development build instead of Expo Go, and the Expo docs say so on each library page.

quiz.q: What should the app do if the user denies camera permission?
Why copy a picked photo into the app's folder?
Where do iOS permission messages come from?

lessons.title: Project 9: Habit Tracker with Streaks and Notifications
lessons.description: Build a habit tracker with streaks calculated from dates, saved data and a daily reminder using expo-notifications and permission handling.

content.text: Habit and reminder apps feel alive because they remember your progress and nudge you at the right time. This project covers two things: a clean way to calculate streaks from dates, and **local notifications**, which the app schedules on the phone itself with no server.
Concepts in this project

items: **Date keys**: store each completed day as a text key such as `2026-11-04`. Text keys avoid time-zone bugs from storing full timestamps.
**Streak function**: a plain function counts consecutive days ending today, or yesterday if today is not done yet, so a streak is not shown as broken during the day.
**Local notifications**: `scheduleNotificationAsync` with a daily trigger fires every day at a set time, even when the app is closed.
**Permission**: ask with `requestPermissionsAsync`. On Android 8 and later you also create a notification channel.
**Notification handler**: tells the app how to show notifications that arrive while it is open.
**Limits**: remote push notifications (sent from a server) need more setup and are outside this lesson. Notifications can behave differently in Expo Go. For a faithful test, use a development build.

content.text: Create the project

items: Use a blank Expo TypeScript project.
Install: `npx expo install expo-notifications @react-native-async-storage/async-storage`.
Add the plugin entry for expo-notifications to `app.json` (see lesson 10's permissions file).
Add `habits.ts` and `reminders.ts`, and replace `App.tsx`.

content.text: **`habits.ts`**
**`reminders.ts`**
**`App.tsx`**
How it works

items: `dayKey` makes the date key. `streak` walks backwards from today while days are in the set.
Marking done toggles today's key in the habit's list. The streak is calculated while rendering, not stored.
The reminder switch asks for permission, cancels old reminders and schedules one daily at 8 pm. Turning it off cancels all of them.
If permission is refused, the switch stays off and an alert explains how to fix it.

content.text: The notification trigger format has changed between Expo SDK versions. This code uses the typed form. If your editor reports a type error on `trigger`, check the expo-notifications page in the Expo docs for your SDK.
Expected output

The screen shows Habits, a reminder switch and a box to add habits. Add Read and Walk. Press Mark done on Read: the button turns green and says Done, and the line reads "1 day streak". Press it again to undo. Turn on the reminder: a permission request appears. Allow it. At 8 pm each day you receive a notification titled Habit check-in. To test faster, change the hour and minute to a time a minute or two ahead. Close and reopen the app: habits and streaks remain.

The code in this course was syntax-checked with a TypeScript parser. It was not run on a phone or emulator while the course was written, so type it in, run it with Expo and fix any small differences your versions show. Always install Expo libraries with `npx expo install` so the versions match your Expo SDK.
Your task

items: Build the app, add two habits and mark one done.
Schedule the reminder for two minutes ahead and confirm that it arrives.
Deny the permission once and check that the app handles it.
Run the streak tests from the testing lesson.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Streaks and habits persist.
The reminder arrives on a device.
You can explain why dates are stored as text keys.

steps.say: The user marks a habit done and today's date key is added.
The streak function counts back through consecutive days.
A separate daily reminder is scheduled once, with permission.
Each evening the phone shows the notification, even if the app is closed.

faqs.q: Local or push notifications?
faqs.a: Local notifications are scheduled by the app on the phone and need no server. Push notifications are sent from a server to many devices, and need a token and a backend.

faqs.q: Why not store timestamps?
faqs.a: A timestamp depends on the time zone. A date key like 2026-11-04 means the same day for the user no matter when you read it.

faqs.q: Why is my notification late or missing?
faqs.a: Check permission, battery saver settings and the channel on Android, and the Focus modes on iPhone. Test on a real device, not an emulator.

quiz.q: Why store completed days as text keys like 2026-11-04?
What is a local notification?
options: One the app schedules on the phone, without a server
One sent from a server only

quiz.q: Why pass the date into the streak function?
options: It makes the function easy to test

lessons.title: Project 10 Capstone: Shop App with Zustand and Tabs
lessons.description: Build a shop app capstone with a product grid, category filter, a Zustand cart store, tab navigation with a live cart count and a demo checkout.

content.text: The last project brings together a typical shop: products from an API, filters, a cart and two tabs. It adds **Zustand**, a small, popular state library. A cart is a good example of global state because many screens read and change it, and the tab bar even shows its count.
Concepts in this project

items: **Zustand store**: `create` makes a store with state and actions. Components read what they need with a selector like `useCart((s) => s.add)`, and re-render only when that part changes.
**Selectors and derived data**: `cartCount` and `cartTotal` are plain functions over the lines, so they cannot go out of date.
**Tabs**: `Tabs` from Expo Router gives a bottom tab bar. The Cart tab label shows the live count.
**FlatList grid**: `numColumns={2}` makes a product grid. A horizontal FlatList shows category chips.
**TanStack Query** loads the products (project 7).
**Data source**: the Fake Store API at fakestoreapi.com. It is a free practice API, so check that it is still online. Prices are demo values, and the checkout here only clears the cart.

content.text: Create the project

items: Use an Expo Router project.
Install: `npm install zustand @tanstack/react-query`.
Create the files below. Note that `cart.ts` (the store) lives in `src`, and `cart.tsx` (the screen) lives in `app`.

content.text:
my-app/
  app/
    _layout.tsx    Tabs + QueryClientProvider
    index.tsx      Shop tab: products
    cart.tsx       Cart tab
  src/
    api.ts         fetchProducts
    cart.ts        the Zustand store
**`src/cart.ts`**
**`src/api.ts`**
**`app/_layout.tsx`**
**`app/index.tsx`**
**`app/cart.tsx`**
How it works

items: `add` increases the quantity if the product is already in the cart, or adds a new line. `decrease` removes a line when its quantity reaches zero. `flatMap` makes that easy.
The shop reads only `add` from the store, so it does not redraw when quantities change elsewhere.
The cart tab label reads the count with a selector and updates instantly.
Place demo order clears the cart. A real checkout needs a payment provider and a server, which this app does not include.

content.text: Expected output

The Shop tab shows category chips (All and the categories from the API) above a two-column grid of products with pictures, titles and prices. Tap Add to cart on two products: the tab shows Cart (2). Open the Cart tab: the lines show images, titles, line prices and − and + buttons. Press + on a line and the total goes up. Press − until the quantity is zero and the line disappears. Press the ✕ to remove a line. Place demo order empties the cart.

The code in this course was syntax-checked with a TypeScript parser. It was not run on a phone or emulator while the course was written, so type it in, run it with Expo and fix any small differences your versions show. Always install Expo libraries with `npx expo install` so the versions match your Expo SDK.
Your task

items: Build the app and fill the cart from two categories.
Persist the cart with Zustand's `persist` middleware and AsyncStorage.
Add a product detail screen with a larger image and description.
Add a promo code text box that applies a fixed discount, and show the saved amount.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The cart count in the tab bar matches the items.
Quantities and totals stay correct as you tap + and −.
You can explain why a selector keeps screens from redrawing.

steps.say: The user taps Add to cart on a product.
The action updates the store.
The tab label reads the count from the store and shows Cart (2).
The Cart tab reads the same lines and total, so all screens agree.

faqs.q: Zustand, Redux or Context?
faqs.a: Context is fine for small shared state. Zustand is lighter than Redux, has less code and avoids needless re-renders with selectors. Redux Toolkit is common in big teams, so it is worth reading about.

faqs.q: Why use selectors?
faqs.a: A selector subscribes a component to only one piece of the store. The component redraws only when that piece changes.

faqs.q: How would I add real payments?
faqs.a: Use a payment provider's official SDK or hosted checkout and a server that creates orders. Never handle card numbers yourself.

quiz.q: What does a Zustand selector do?
options: Subscribes a component to one part of the store

quiz.q: Why derive the cart total with a function over the lines?
options: It cannot go out of date

quiz.q: What does the demo checkout do in this app?
options: Clears the cart; no real payment

lessons.title: Forms, Validation, Secure Storage and Authentication
lessons.description: Build React Native forms with validation, store tokens safely with expo-secure-store and design login flows with protected routes in Expo Router.

content.text: Almost every real app needs a login or sign-up form, and the data it handles is sensitive. This lesson shows how to build forms that give clear feedback, where to store a login token, and how to protect screens. It uses short examples that you can add to the apps you built. It does not need a project of its own.
Forms and validation
A form is state plus rules. Keep each field in state, validate on submit (and on blur for a nicer feel) and show the message next to the field. Return errors from a plain function so you can test it.

Use the right keyboard type, turn off auto-capitalisation for emails, and `secureTextEntry` for passwords. Wrap long forms in `KeyboardAvoidingView` and a `ScrollView` with `keyboardShouldPersistTaps="handled"` so the keyboard does not hide the fields. For big forms, libraries such as React Hook Form with a schema validator like Zod save work.
Client-side checks are for user experience only. The server must validate everything again, because anyone can send requests without your app.
Where to store a token

After login, your server returns a token that proves who the user is. AsyncStorage is not encrypted, so it is not the place for it. Use **expo-secure-store**, which keeps values in the iOS Keychain and the Android Keystore.

Install it with `npx expo install expo-secure-store`. Keep tokens short-lived and refresh them as your backend allows. Send them in a header, never in the URL: `fetch(url, { headers: { Authorization: \`Bearer \${token}\` } })`.
Protecting screens
A simple pattern with Expo Router keeps signed-in screens in one group and redirects when there is no session. Keep the session in a small Context or Zustand store that loads the token at start.
Files under `app/(app)/` are protected, and `app/login.tsx` stays open. The parentheses make a group that does not appear in the URL.
Security habits

items: Never put secrets, private keys or API keys with write power in the app.
Use HTTPS only.
Never log passwords or tokens.
Do not trust data from the client on the server.
For social login, use the provider's official method (such as expo-auth-session) rather than building your own.

content.text: These snippets were not run in a full project here. Treat them as patterns to adapt, and test the login flow with your own backend.
Your task

items: Add the validation function and form to a new login screen in one of your projects.
Write three tests for `validateLogin` (bad email, short password, valid input).
Store a fake token with SecureStore after pressing Sign in and read it on app start.
Make a protected group and check that you are redirected when no token exists.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: Invalid input shows messages without a request being sent.
The token is saved in secure storage, not AsyncStorage.
Protected screens redirect to the login screen.

steps.say: The form checks the fields and shows messages for mistakes.
Valid input goes to the server over HTTPS, which checks the password.
The server returns a token, which the app keeps in Keychain or Keystore.
Protected screens read the token. Without it they redirect to login.

faqs.q: Why not keep the token in AsyncStorage?
faqs.a: AsyncStorage is plain, unencrypted storage. SecureStore uses the operating system's secure storage, which is much harder for other apps or tools to read.

faqs.q: Is client-side validation enough?
faqs.a: No. It improves the experience, but a server must validate every request because attackers can skip your app.

faqs.q: Should I build my own login server?
faqs.a: Most teams use a trusted service or a well-tested library for authentication rather than writing password handling themselves.

quiz.q: Where should a login token be stored?
Is client-side validation enough?
options: No, the server must validate too

quiz.q: How does a protected group of screens work in Expo Router?
options: A layout redirects to login when there is no token

lessons.title: Testing and Performance for React Native Apps
lessons.metaTitle: Testing and Performance for React Native
lessons.description: Set up Jest and React Native Testing Library, test pure functions and components, and learn practical performance habits for FlatList, memoisation and images.

content.text: Tests are small programs that check your code automatically. They let you change code without fear and catch mistakes before users do. React Native projects use **Jest** to run tests and **React Native Testing Library** to render components and act like a user: find text, type and press.
Set up testing
**Terminal and package.json**
Test files go in a `__tests__` folder or end in `.test.ts` or `.test.tsx`. `npm test` runs them all.
Test pure functions first

The best tests are for plain functions: the tip maths, the money helpers and the streak counter. They are fast and need no phone. Each test has a name that says what should happen, then a setup, an action and a check.
**`__tests__/tip.test.ts`**
**`__tests__/money.test.ts`**
**`__tests__/streak.test.ts`**

`it.each` runs the same check for many inputs. Notice that the streak test passes the date in as a parameter. Code that takes the current time from outside is far easier to test than code that reads the clock itself.
Test a component
This test renders the tip calculator from project 1, types a bill like a user and checks the visible result. Place `tip.ts` and `App.tsx` at the project root so the imports match.
**`__tests__/TipScreen.test.tsx`**
Find elements by what the user sees (text, placeholder, role) rather than by internal details. If you must target something with no text, give it a `testID` and use `getByTestId`.

The code in this course was syntax-checked with a TypeScript parser. It was not run on a phone or emulator while the course was written, so type it in, run it with Expo and fix any small differences your versions show. Always install Expo libraries with `npx expo install` so the versions match your Expo SDK.

Component tests for screens that use native modules (SQLite, camera, notifications) need those modules mocked. Test their logic through the small functions around them instead, as the data layers in this course allow.
Performance habits

items: **Use FlatList, not ScrollView, for long lists.** Give it a stable `keyExtractor`. For very large lists, tune `initialNumToRender` and `windowSize`, or try a faster list library such as FlashList.
**Keep render cheap.** Do heavy calculations outside render or wrap them in `useMemo`.
**Memoise rows when needed.** `React.memo` on a row component, and `useCallback` for handlers you pass to it, avoid redrawing every row.
**Do not create huge inline objects** or functions inside long lists when a stable reference will do.
**Size images properly.** Do not load a 4000 pixel photo into a 100 pixel thumbnail. Consider the expo-image library for caching.
**Measure, do not guess.** Use the React DevTools Profiler and the performance monitor in the developer menu to see slow renders and dropped frames.
**Test the release build.** Development mode is slower than a release build, so judge speed on a release build.

content.text: Preventing crashes

items: Handle every network, storage and permission error with a visible message.
Use TypeScript and optional chaining for data that might be missing.
Wrap risky screens with an error boundary, or use the error boundary Expo Router provides per route.
Test with a slow network, airplane mode, large text and dark mode.

content.text: Your task

items: Set up Jest and run the three function tests.
Add a test for a case you can think of that is not covered.
Run the component test and add a second one for the round-up switch.
Break a function on purpose, see the test fail, then fix it.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: `npm test` passes.
You can explain why pure functions are easy to test.
You can name three ways to keep a long list smooth.

steps.say: Most tests check plain functions. They run in milliseconds.
Component tests render a screen and act like a user.
A few checks on a real device catch what mocks cannot, such as camera and notifications.
When all pass, you can release with more confidence.

faqs.q: Jest or Vitest?
faqs.a: React Native projects use Jest through the jest-expo preset, because it handles the native environment for you.

faqs.q: How many tests should I write?
faqs.a: Cover rules that would hurt if they broke: money, validation, streaks and state changes. Do not chase 100 percent coverage of simple screens.

faqs.q: Why is my list slow only in development?
faqs.a: Development builds include extra checks and are slower. Always judge speed on a release build on a real phone.

quiz.q: Which tests are the fastest and easiest to write?
options: Tests that need a physical device

quiz.q: Which list component should you use for a long list?
Where should you judge app speed?
options: In a development build on an emulator
In a release build on a real phone

lessons.title: Build and Publish with EAS, and React Native Interviews
lessons.metaTitle: Publish React Native Apps with EAS
lessons.description: Prepare a React Native app for release: app.json, EAS Build for Android and iOS, store submission, over-the-air updates and interview questions.

content.text: An app only matters when people can install it. Expo's build service, **EAS** (Expo Application Services), turns your project into real app files in the cloud, so you do not need Xcode or Android Studio on your computer. Store steps and fees change from time to time, so follow the current instructions from Apple, Google and Expo if they differ from this lesson.
Prepare the app

items: Open `app.json` and set a clear `name`, a unique `slug` and a `version`.
Set a unique app ID for each platform: `ios.bundleIdentifier` and `android.package`, such as `com.yourname.shop`. They cannot be changed after you publish.
Replace the default icon and splash screen in `assets/`.
Check every permission text, and remove libraries and code you do not use.
Test the whole app on at least one real phone.

content.text: Build with EAS
**Terminal commands**

npm install -g eas-cli
eas login
eas build:configure

# test builds you can share
eas build --platform android --profile preview     # APK for testers
eas build --platform ios --profile preview         # needs an Apple Developer account

# store builds
eas build --platform android --profile production  # AAB for Google Play
eas build --platform ios --profile production
eas submit --platform android
eas submit --platform ios

# send a small JavaScript-only fix to installed apps
npx expo install expo-updates
eas update --branch production --message "Fix typo"

items: Create a free Expo account and run `eas login`.
Run `eas build:configure`. It creates an `eas.json` with build profiles.
Build a **preview** version first. For Android this is an APK you can send to testers. For iOS, internal builds need an Apple Developer account.
Install it on a phone and check the whole app, because release builds can behave differently from Expo Go.
Build the **production** version: an AAB for Google Play and an IPA for the App Store. EAS can manage signing credentials for you, or you can supply your own.

content.text: Some libraries, such as ones with custom native code, do not run in Expo Go. A **development build** (`eas build --profile development`) is a custom version of Expo Go that includes them.
Publish to the stores

items: **Google Play**: create a Play Console developer account (a one-time fee applies). Create the app, fill in the store listing, privacy policy, data safety and content rating forms, upload the AAB to an Internal testing track, then move to Production when ready. New personal accounts may have extra testing requirements, so check the current rules.

**App Store**: join the Apple Developer Program (a yearly fee applies). Create the app in App Store Connect, add screenshots, a description and privacy details, upload the build, test with TestFlight, then submit for review.
`eas submit` can upload builds to both stores from the command line.
Reviews can take days. Fix any feedback and resubmit.

content.text: Over-the-air updates

With `expo-updates` you can send a JavaScript or asset fix directly to installed apps, without a full store review, using `eas update`. It cannot change native code, so changes to native libraries or permissions still need a new build. Stores also have rules about what updates may change, so keep them to bug fixes and small improvements.
After release

items: Read reviews and fix problems fast.
Add crash reporting (for example Sentry) so you see errors from real devices.
Raise the version, and the build number, for every release.
Keep Expo SDK and libraries reasonably current. Upgrade with `npx expo install --fix` and the SDK upgrade guide.

content.text: Interview preparation
Interviewers want to hear that you understand how React Native works and can explain choices. Practise answering these aloud with examples from your own projects.

items: What is React Native and how is it different from a hybrid web app?
What is Expo and when would you use a development build or bare React Native?
Explain props, state and the rules of hooks.
What does `useEffect` do, and what does the dependency array mean?
How does `FlatList` work, and how do you make a long list fast?
How does Flexbox in React Native differ from the web?
How do you store data on the device? AsyncStorage, SQLite and SecureStore: when do you use each?
What is the difference between server state and client state, and what tools do you use?
How do you handle permissions properly?
How do you test a React Native app?
How do you share navigation params, and why are they strings in Expo Router?
What is the new architecture of React Native (Fabric and TurboModules) and what problem does it solve?

content.text: Make a short portfolio: publish three or four of the ten apps to GitHub with a README, screenshots and the steps to run them. Add one that is on a store or in TestFlight if you can. Honest, working projects matter more than a long list of tools.

The code in this course was syntax-checked with a TypeScript parser. It was not run on a phone or emulator while the course was written, so type it in, run it with Expo and fix any small differences your versions show. Always install Expo libraries with `npx expo install` so the versions match your Expo SDK.
Your task

items: Pick your best project and set its name, icon and app IDs in `app.json`.
Run `eas build:configure` and make a preview build for Android.
Install the build on a phone and write down anything that differs from Expo Go.
Answer five of the interview questions aloud and note the ones you could not answer.

content.text: How to check it worked

items: The preview build installs and runs on a real phone.
You know the difference between an EAS update and a new build.
You can describe the steps from code to store in order.

steps.say: You finish and test the app and set its name, icon and app IDs.
EAS Build compiles signed Android and iOS files in the cloud.
You submit the builds to Google Play and the App Store for review.
People install the app. Small JavaScript fixes can follow as over-the-air updates.

faqs.q: Do I need a Mac to publish to the App Store?
faqs.a: No. EAS Build compiles iOS apps in the cloud. You still need an Apple Developer account, and you can upload with eas submit.

faqs.q: What is the difference between eas build and eas update?
faqs.a: A build creates a new app file for the stores. An update sends changed JavaScript and assets to apps that are already installed, but cannot change native code.

faqs.q: How do I get my first React Native job?
faqs.a: Publish a few real projects on GitHub, make one polished app, practise the interview questions above, and apply for junior and internship roles while you keep building.

quiz.q: What does EAS Build do?
options: Builds signed app files in the cloud

quiz.q: What can an EAS update change?
options: JavaScript and assets, not native code
Only the app icon in the store

quiz.q: What format does Google Play need for production?
